course.title: Spanish, Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: Latin American Spanish from real-world basics through fluent, everyday command — real sentences, real grammar, real conversation
course.heroNative: De lo esencial a la fluidez
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real sentences from lesson one, with genuine native-quality audio for every single line.

a2-reflexive.title: Reflexive Verbs: me, te, se...
a2-reflexive.explanation: Many everyday Spanish verbs describing routines are reflexive: the action is done TO oneself, so a small pronoun (me/te/se/nos/se) goes right before the verb. "Levantarse" (to get (oneself) up) becomes "me levanto" (I get up), "te levantas" (you get up), "se levanta" (he/she gets up). The pronoun changes with the subject but the verb conjugates completely normally otherwise.
a2-reflexive.fact: Spanish uses reflexive verbs for far more than literal self-actions — "llamarse" (to call oneself) is simply how you say your name ("Me llamo Ana" = "My name is Ana"), and many emotional/change-of-state verbs are reflexive too ("enojarse" = to get angry, "aburrirse" = to get bored) even though English doesn't treat them as reflexive at all.

dialogue.native: ¿A qué hora te levantas?
dialogue.en: What time do you get up?

dialogue.native: Me levanto a las seis y media.
dialogue.en: I get up at six thirty.

a2-preterite.title: The Preterite: Completed Past Actions
a2-preterite.explanation: The preterite describes an action that was completed at a specific point in the past — something that started and finished, like a single event. Regular -ar verbs add -é/-aste/-ó/-amos/-aron (hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron); regular -er and -ir verbs share the same endings: -í/-iste/-ió/-imos/-ieron (comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron).
a2-preterite.fact: Many of Spanish's most common verbs are irregular in the preterite and simply have to be memorized: "ir" (to go) and "ser" (to be) share the exact same preterite forms (fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron) — context alone tells you which one is meant. "Hacer" becomes hice/hiciste/hizo/hicimos/hicieron, and "tener" becomes tuve/tuviste/tuvo/tuvimos/tuvieron.

dialogue.native: ¿Qué hiciste ayer?
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.native: Fui al cine con mis amigos.
dialogue.en: I went to the movies with my friends.

a2-imperfect.title: The Imperfect: Ongoing or Habitual Past
a2-imperfect.explanation: While the preterite marks a completed event, the imperfect describes what was ongoing, habitual, or in the background — "used to" or "was ...ing" in English. Regular -ar verbs add -aba/-abas/-aba/-ábamos/-aban (hablaba, hablabas...); -er and -ir verbs share -ía/-ías/-ía/-íamos/-ían (comía, vivía...). Only three verbs are irregular in the imperfect: ser (era, eras, era, éramos, eran), ir (iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, iban), and ver (veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veían).
a2-imperfect.fact: The imperfect is what sets the scene: "Cuando era niño, vivía en el campo" (When I was a child, I lived in the countryside) describes an ongoing state, not a single completed event — that's exactly why "era" and "vivía" are imperfect, not preterite. A sentence often mixes both: the imperfect describes what was happening, and the preterite marks the single event that interrupted it.

dialogue.native: ¿Cómo era tu vida cuando eras joven?
dialogue.en: What was your life like when you were young?

dialogue.native: Vivía en un pueblo pequeño y jugaba mucho afuera.
dialogue.en: I lived in a small town and played outside a lot.

a2-ser-estar.title: Ser vs. Estar: Two Ways to Say "To Be"
a2-ser-estar.pattern: ser = identity, characteristics, origin, time · estar = location, condition, ongoing states
a2-ser-estar.explanation: Spanish splits "to be" into two verbs. "Ser" is for things that define what something fundamentally IS: identity ("Soy Ana"), permanent characteristics ("Es alta"), origin ("Es de México"), profession, and time ("Son las tres"). "Estar" is for location ("Estoy en casa") and temporary states or conditions ("Estoy cansado", "La sopa está caliente").
a2-ser-estar.fact: The same adjective can take either verb with a real difference in meaning: "Ella es aburrida" means "She is boring" (a trait), while "Ella está aburrida" means "She is bored" (a temporary feeling) — one small verb swap changes the whole sentence.

dialogue.native: ¿Cómo estás?
dialogue.en: How are you (feeling)?

dialogue.native: Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú de dónde eres?
dialogue.en: I'm well, thanks. And where are you from?

a2-direct-object.title: Direct Object Pronouns: lo, la, los, las
a2-direct-object.explanation: A direct object pronoun replaces the thing or person directly receiving the action, and in Spanish it goes BEFORE the conjugated verb (the opposite order from English). "Compro el pan" (I buy the bread) becomes "Lo compro" (I buy it) — "pan" is masculine so it's replaced by "lo". Feminine nouns use "la", and the plurals are "los" and "las".
a2-direct-object.fact: With two verbs together (like wanting + an infinitive), the pronoun can go in either of two places with no change in meaning: before the first verb ("Lo quiero comprar") or attached to the end of the infinitive ("Quiero comprarlo") — both mean exactly "I want to buy it".

dialogue.native: ¿Ya compraste los boletos?
dialogue.en: Did you already buy the tickets?

dialogue.native: Sí, los compré esta mañana.
dialogue.en: Yes, I bought them this morning.

a2-gustar.title: Gustar: "To Be Pleasing To"
a2-gustar.explanation: "Gustar" doesn't work like English "to like" — literally it means "to be pleasing to", so the THING liked is the grammatical subject, and the PERSON who likes it takes an indirect object pronoun. "Me gusta el café" is literally "Coffee is pleasing to me." The verb agrees with the thing liked: "gusta" for one thing, "gustan" for several ("Me gustan los libros").
a2-gustar.fact: Several other very common verbs work exactly the same way: "encantar" (to love/be delighted by), "interesar" (to interest), "molestar" (to bother), "faltar" (to be lacking) — once you understand "me gusta", all of these follow the identical [pronoun] + verb + [thing] pattern.

dialogue.native: ¿Te gusta el fútbol?
dialogue.en: Do you like soccer?

dialogue.native: Sí, me encanta. Me gustan mucho los partidos los fines de semana.
dialogue.en: Yes, I love it. I really like the games on weekends.

a2-indirect-object.title: Indirect Object Pronouns: me, te, le, nos, les
a2-indirect-object.explanation: An indirect object pronoun marks WHO receives or benefits from an action — usually the person a thing is given, told, or shown to. "Le doy el regalo a mi madre" (I give the gift to my mother) can simply be "Le doy el regalo" once context is clear — "le" already means "to her/him/you-formal". Unlike direct object pronouns, "le" and "les" don't change for gender.
a2-indirect-object.fact: "Le" is ambiguous on its own (it can mean to him, to her, or to you-formal), so Spanish often adds "a él", "a ella", or the person's name for clarity even though the pronoun is technically already there: "Le escribí una carta a mi abuela" keeps both "le" and "a mi abuela" together, which sounds redundant to English speakers but is completely normal and expected in Spanish.

dialogue.native: ¿Le compraste algo a tu hermana?
dialogue.en: Did you buy something for your sister?

dialogue.native: Sí, le compré un libro que le va a encantar.
dialogue.en: Yes, I bought her a book that she's going to love.

a2-ir-a.title: Ir a + Infinitive: Talking About the Near Future
a2-ir-a.explanation: The easiest and most common way to talk about future plans in everyday Spanish isn't a special future tense at all — it's just "ir" (to go), conjugated, plus "a", plus an infinitive: "Voy a estudiar" (I am going to study), "Vamos a viajar" (We are going to travel). It works exactly like English "going to".
a2-ir-a.fact: This construction is used constantly in spoken Latin American Spanish — far more often than the formal future tense (like "estudiaré"), which tends to sound a bit more formal or literary in everyday conversation. If you only ever learn one way to talk about the future, "ir a + infinitive" is the one that gets used the most.

dialogue.native: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.native: Voy a visitar a mis padres y vamos a cocinar juntos.
dialogue.en: I am going to visit my parents and we are going to cook together.

a2-comparatives.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
a2-comparatives.explanation: To compare two things, Spanish uses "más...que" (more...than) or "menos...que" (less...than): "Mi hermano es más alto que yo" (My brother is taller than me). For equal comparisons, use "tan...como" (as...as): "Es tan inteligente como su hermana." For the superlative — the most/least of a group — add the definite article: "el más alto", "la más inteligente".
a2-comparatives.fact: A handful of common adjectives have their own irregular comparative words instead of using "más": "bueno" (good) becomes "mejor" (better), "malo" (bad) becomes "peor" (worse), and "viejo"/"joven" have both a regular form (más viejo/más joven) and, for age among people, the special words "mayor"/"menor".

dialogue.native: ¿Cuál restaurante es mejor, este o aquel?
dialogue.en: Which restaurant is better, this one or that one?

dialogue.native: Este es mejor, pero aquel es más barato.
dialogue.en: This one is better, but that one is cheaper.

b1-commands.title: Commands: Telling People What to Do
b1-commands.pattern: tú: [present-tense él/ella form] · usted: [present subjunctive] · negative: no + subjunctive
b1-commands.explanation: Informal (tú) commands mostly borrow the él/ella present-tense form: "¡Habla!" (Talk!), "¡Come!" (Eat!), "¡Escribe!" (Write!). Formal (usted) commands use the present subjunctive form instead: "¡Hable!", "¡Coma!", "¡Escriba!". Negative commands ALWAYS use the subjunctive, even for tú: "¡No hables!", "¡No comas!".
b1-commands.fact: A handful of very common verbs have irregular tú affirmative commands that don't follow the él/ella-form rule at all: "decir" → "di", "hacer" → "haz", "ir" → "ve", "poner" → "pon", "salir" → "sal", "ser" → "sé", "tener" → "ten", "venir" → "ven" — these eight are simply memorized.

dialogue.native: ¡Ven aquí y ayúdame con esto!
dialogue.en: Come here and help me with this!

dialogue.native: Ya voy, no te preocupes.
dialogue.en: I'm coming, don't worry.

b1-present-perfect.title: Present Perfect: Talking About Recent Experience
b1-present-perfect.explanation: The present perfect connects a past action to now — something that happened recently, or an experience that still matters. Form it with a conjugated form of "haber" plus the past participle: "he hablado" (I have spoken), "has comido" (you have eaten), "ha vivido" (he/she has lived). The participle never changes for gender or number here — it always ends in -ado or -ido.
b1-present-perfect.fact: Several very common verbs have irregular past participles that must be memorized: "hacer" → "hecho", "decir" → "dicho", "ver" → "visto", "poner" → "puesto", "escribir" → "escrito", "volver" → "vuelto", "abrir" → "abierto", "romper" → "roto", "morir" → "muerto".

dialogue.native: ¿Has visto la nueva película de la que todos hablan?
dialogue.en: Have you seen the new movie everyone's talking about?

dialogue.native: No, todavía no he tenido tiempo de verla.
dialogue.en: No, I haven't had time to see it yet.

b1-subjunctive-intro.title: Present Subjunctive: Wishes, Wants, and Doubts
b1-subjunctive-intro.pattern: querer/esperar/necesitar que + [subject] + subjunctive verb (-e for -ar verbs, -a for -er/-ir verbs)
b1-subjunctive-intro.explanation: When one subject wants, hopes, or needs another subject to do something, Spanish switches the second verb into the subjunctive mood after "que": "Quiero que vengas" (I want you to come), "Espero que estés bien" (I hope you're well), "Necesito que me ayudes" (I need you to help me). The subjunctive endings flip the usual pattern: -ar verbs take -e endings, -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.
b1-subjunctive-intro.fact: The subjunctive is only used when the subject of "querer"/"esperar" and the subject of the second verb are DIFFERENT people. If they're the same person, Spanish just uses an infinitive instead: "Quiero ir" (I want to go — not "quiero que vaya"), but "Quiero que vayas" (I want you to go).

dialogue.native: Espero que puedas venir a mi fiesta el sábado.
dialogue.en: I hope you can come to my party on Saturday.

dialogue.native: Claro, quiero que sea una noche inolvidable.
dialogue.en: Of course, I want it to be an unforgettable night.

b1-relative-clauses.title: Relative Clauses: Connecting Ideas with que, quien, donde
b1-relative-clauses.pattern: que (that/which/who) · quien(es) (who, after a preposition) · donde (where)
b1-relative-clauses.explanation: "Que" is the all-purpose relative pronoun for both people and things: "el libro que leí" (the book that I read), "la mujer que conocí" (the woman I met). "Quien"/"quienes" refers only to people and is used mainly after a preposition: "la persona con quien hablé" (the person with whom I spoke). "Donde" replaces a place: "la casa donde nací" (the house where I was born).
b1-relative-clauses.fact: Unlike English, Spanish never drops the relative pronoun. English allows "the book I read" with no "that," but Spanish always requires "el libro que leí" — "que" can never be omitted.

dialogue.native: Esta es la ciudad donde crecí.
dialogue.en: This is the city where I grew up.

dialogue.native: ¿Y quién es esa persona con quien estás hablando?
dialogue.en: And who is that person you're talking with?

b1-por-para.title: Por vs Para: Two Words for 'For'
b1-por-para.explanation: "Por" looks backward to a cause, means, or exchange: "Gracias por tu ayuda" (thanks for your help — cause), "Viajamos por tren" (we traveled by train — means), "Pagué veinte dólares por el libro" (I paid twenty dollars for the book — exchange). "Para" looks forward to a purpose, destination, or deadline: "Este regalo es para ti" (this gift is for you — recipient), "Salgo para Madrid mañana" (I leave for Madrid tomorrow — destination), "Necesito esto para el lunes" (I need this by Monday — deadline).
b1-por-para.fact: A useful shortcut: "por" often answers "why/how," while "para" answers "for what purpose/for whom." "Trabajo por dinero" (I work because of/for the sake of money) versus "Trabajo para una empresa grande" (I work for a big company — the employer, not the motive).

dialogue.native: ¿Para quién es este paquete?
dialogue.en: Who is this package for?

dialogue.native: Es para mi madre, lo compré por su cumpleaños.
dialogue.en: It's for my mother, I bought it for her birthday.

b1-past-perfect.title: Past Perfect: An Action Before Another Past Action
b1-past-perfect.explanation: The past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) describes something that had already happened before another point in the past: "Cuando llegué, ya habían empezado la reunión" (when I arrived, they had already started the meeting). It's built with the imperfect of "haber" plus the past participle, and it's what lets you clearly sequence two past events.
b1-past-perfect.fact: The same irregular participles from the present perfect carry over unchanged: "había hecho", "había visto", "había dicho", "había puesto" — if you know the present perfect's irregulars, the past perfect uses exactly the same set.

dialogue.native: Cuando llegamos al cine, la película ya había comenzado.
dialogue.en: When we got to the movies, the film had already started.

dialogue.native: ¡Qué mal! Nunca había llegado tan tarde.
dialogue.en: That's too bad! I had never arrived so late.

b1plus-future.title: Future Tense: What Will Happen
b1plus-future.explanation: The future tense attaches endings directly onto the infinitive, the same endings for -ar/-er/-ir verbs: "hablaré" (I will speak), "comerás" (you will eat), "vivirá" (he/she will live). It's used for predictions and plans, and also — a distinctly Spanish use — to express probability about the present: "¿Qué hora será?" (I wonder what time it is / What time could it be?).
b1plus-future.fact: About a dozen common verbs have an irregular future stem while keeping the regular endings: "tener" → "tendr-", "poner" → "pondr-", "salir" → "saldr-", "venir" → "vendr-", "decir" → "dir-", "hacer" → "har-", "poder" → "podr-", "querer" → "querr-", "saber" → "sabr-" — so "tendré", "haré", "podrás", etc.

dialogue.native: ¿Crees que lloverá mañana?
dialogue.en: Do you think it will rain tomorrow?

dialogue.native: No lo sé, pero llevaré un paraguas por si acaso.
dialogue.en: I don't know, but I'll bring an umbrella just in case.

b1plus-conditional.title: Conditional Tense: What Would Happen
b1plus-conditional.explanation: The conditional uses the same stems as the future (including the same irregulars) but swaps in the imperfect-style -ía endings: "hablaría" (I would speak), "tendría" (I would have), "haría" (I would do). It expresses hypothetical actions, polite requests, and past-projected future ("dijo que vendría" — he said he would come).
b1plus-conditional.fact: "Me gustaría" (I would like) is the most common conditional phrase in everyday Spanish — softer and more polite than "quiero" (I want), much like English "I would like" versus "I want."

dialogue.native: ¿Qué harías tú en mi situación?
dialogue.en: What would you do in my situation?

dialogue.native: Yo hablaría con ella directamente, sería lo más honesto.
dialogue.en: I would talk to her directly, it would be the most honest thing.

b1plus-passive.title: Passive Voice: When the Subject Receives the Action
b1plus-passive.pattern: ser + past participle (agrees in gender/number) · se + verb (impersonal passive)
b1plus-passive.explanation: Formal passive voice uses "ser" plus a past participle that AGREES with the subject: "La carta fue escrita por Ana" (The letter was written by Ana), "Los premios serán entregados mañana" (The prizes will be given out tomorrow). Everyday spoken Spanish more often uses the "se pasiva" instead: "Se venden casas" (Houses [are] sold / For sale), "Se habla español aquí" (Spanish is spoken here) — no agent mentioned, and the verb agrees with the noun that follows.
b1plus-passive.fact: The "se pasiva" is everywhere on real signs and everyday speech — "Se prohíbe fumar" (Smoking is prohibited), "Se busca camarero" (Waiter wanted) — while the "ser + participle" passive sounds more formal and is common in news writing and formal reports.

dialogue.native: ¿Sabes si se aceptan tarjetas de crédito aquí?
dialogue.en: Do you know if credit cards are accepted here?

dialogue.native: Creo que sí, pero el menú fue actualizado la semana pasada, mejor pregunta.
dialogue.en: I think so, but the menu was updated last week, better ask.

b1plus-indirect-speech.title: Indirect Speech: Reporting What Someone Said
b1plus-indirect-speech.pattern: decir/preguntar que + [reported clause, tense shifted back one step]
b1plus-indirect-speech.explanation: When you report what someone said, the verb tense usually shifts back one step: present becomes imperfect ("Tengo hambre" → dijo que tenía hambre), present perfect becomes past perfect ("He terminado" → dijo que había terminado), future becomes conditional ("Vendré" → dijo que vendría). Questions use "si" for yes/no questions or the question word directly: "me preguntó si vendría" (she asked me if I would come), "me preguntó dónde vivía" (she asked me where I lived).
b1plus-indirect-speech.fact: If the reporting verb is in the present tense ("dice que..."), no tense shift is needed at all — the shift only happens when reporting from a past-tense perspective ("dijo que..."), because that's when the original statement's "now" has already moved into the past.

dialogue.native: ¿Qué te dijo el médico?
dialogue.en: What did the doctor tell you?

dialogue.native: Me dijo que descansara y que volviera si no mejoraba.
dialogue.en: He told me to rest and to come back if I didn't get better.

b1plus-subjunctive-deeper.title: Subjunctive Beyond Wishes: Purpose, Concession, Conditions
b1plus-subjunctive-deeper.pattern: para que / sin que / antes de que / aunque / a menos que + subjunctive
b1plus-subjunctive-deeper.explanation: Certain connectors always trigger the subjunctive in the clause that follows, because they introduce something not yet realized or hypothetical: "para que" (so that) — "Te lo explico para que entiendas"; "antes de que" (before) — "Llama antes de que sea tarde"; "sin que" (without) — "Salió sin que nadie lo viera"; "a menos que" (unless) — "No iré a menos que me acompañes." "Aunque" (although/even if) takes the subjunctive specifically when the concession is hypothetical or unconfirmed, and the indicative when it's an accepted fact.
b1plus-subjunctive-deeper.fact: "Ojalá" (I wish / hopefully), borrowed from Arabic "law šā' allāh" (God willing) centuries ago during the Moorish period in Spain, ALWAYS takes the subjunctive and is one of the most common ways to express a wish in everyday Spanish: "Ojalá que ganemos" (I hope we win).

dialogue.native: Aunque llueva, vamos a ir a la playa.
dialogue.en: Even if it rains, we're going to go to the beach.

dialogue.native: Ojalá que salga el sol, sería perfecto.
dialogue.en: I hope the sun comes out, it would be perfect.

b2-imperfect-subjunctive.title: Imperfect Subjunctive: The Hypothetical Past
b2-imperfect-subjunctive.explanation: Take any verb's "ellos" preterite form, drop "-ron", and add these endings: "hablaron" → "hablara", "tuvieron" → "tuviera", "fueron" → "fuera". Because it's built from the preterite stem, it automatically inherits all of the preterite's irregulars — no separate irregular list to learn. It's used after past-tense subjunctive triggers ("quería que vinieras" — I wanted you to come) and in hypothetical "si" clauses about the present ("si tuviera tiempo..." — if I had time...).
b2-imperfect-subjunctive.fact: There's a second, less common ending set (-se instead of -ra: "hablase", "tuviese") that means exactly the same thing and is more common in Spain and in literary writing; Latin American speech overwhelmingly favors the -ra forms, which is why this course uses -ra throughout.

dialogue.native: Si tuviera más tiempo libre, aprendería a tocar el piano.
dialogue.en: If I had more free time, I would learn to play piano.

dialogue.native: Yo también quería que mis padres me obligaran a aprender de niño.
dialogue.en: I also wish my parents had made me learn as a kid.

b2-si-clauses.title: Si-Clauses: Hypothetical Present and Unreal Past
b2-si-clauses.pattern: Type 2: si + imperfect subjunctive, + conditional · Type 3: si + pluperfect subjunctive, + conditional perfect
b2-si-clauses.explanation: For a hypothetical or contrary-to-fact PRESENT situation, use "si" + imperfect subjunctive in the "si" clause, and the conditional in the result: "Si tuviera tiempo, iría" (If I had time, I would go — but I don't). For an unreal PAST situation, go one step further back: "si" + pluperfect subjunctive ("hubiera" + participle) with the conditional perfect ("habría" + participle) in the result: "Si hubiera tenido tiempo, habría ido" (If I had had time, I would have gone — but I didn't).
b2-si-clauses.fact: Never use the present subjunctive after "si" for a hypothetical — that's a common learner error. Real, open possibilities use the simple present indicative instead ("si tengo tiempo, voy" — if I have time, I'll go, a genuinely open question), while the subjunctive forms are reserved specifically for situations presented as contrary to fact or unlikely.

dialogue.native: Si hubiera estudiado más, habría aprobado el examen.
dialogue.en: If I had studied more, I would have passed the exam.

dialogue.native: Bueno, si practicaras un poco cada día ahora, no tendrías este problema la próxima vez.
dialogue.en: Well, if you practiced a little each day now, you wouldn't have this problem next time.

b2-temporal-subjunctive.title: Subjunctive in Time Clauses: Cuando, Hasta Que, Mientras
b2-temporal-subjunctive.pattern: cuando/hasta que/en cuanto/tan pronto como + subjunctive (future/unrealized) · same connectors + indicative (habitual/past/completed)
b2-temporal-subjunctive.explanation: Time connectors like "cuando" (when), "hasta que" (until), "en cuanto"/"tan pronto como" (as soon as) take the SUBJUNCTIVE when they refer to an action that hasn't happened yet: "Te llamaré cuando llegue" (I'll call you when I arrive — I haven't arrived yet). The same connectors take the INDICATIVE when describing something habitual or already completed: "Siempre te llamo cuando llego" (I always call you when I arrive — habitual fact), "Te llamé cuando llegué" (I called you when I arrived — already happened).
b2-temporal-subjunctive.fact: "Mientras" (while) works similarly: "mientras" + subjunctive for an unrealized simultaneous condition ("mientras tengas paciencia, todo irá bien" — as long as you have patience...), but "mientras" + indicative for a genuinely simultaneous ongoing action ("mientras cocino, escucho música" — while I cook, I listen to music).

dialogue.native: Avísame en cuanto termines el informe.
dialogue.en: Let me know as soon as you finish the report.

dialogue.native: Claro, y normalmente te aviso apenas termino cualquier cosa importante.
dialogue.en: Of course, and I usually let you know as soon as I finish anything important.

b2-advanced-connectors.title: Advanced Connectors: Linking Ideas Like a Native Speaker
b2-advanced-connectors.pattern: sin embargo/no obstante (however) · por lo tanto/así que (therefore) · a pesar de que (despite) · ya que/dado que (since/given that)
b2-advanced-connectors.explanation: These connectors let you build more sophisticated arguments. Contrast: "sin embargo" and "no obstante" both mean "however," typically starting a new sentence. Consequence: "por lo tanto" and "así que" mean "therefore/so." Concession: "a pesar de que" (despite the fact that) is followed by the indicative when the fact is real, subjunctive when hypothetical — just like "aunque." Cause: "ya que" and "dado que" (since/given that) introduce a reason the listener likely already knows, softer than a blunt "porque."
b2-advanced-connectors.fact: "No obstante" and "sin embargo" are largely interchangeable, but "no obstante" skews slightly more formal/written — you'll see it constantly in academic or legal Spanish, while "sin embargo" is the everyday default in both speech and writing.

dialogue.native: El vuelo se retrasó tres horas; sin embargo, llegamos a tiempo para la boda.
dialogue.en: The flight was delayed three hours; however, we arrived in time for the wedding.

dialogue.native: Qué suerte, ya que la boda empezaba a las seis en punto.
dialogue.en: What luck, since the wedding started at six sharp.

b2plus-ser-estar-nuanced.title: Ser vs Estar: Beyond the Basic Rule
b2plus-ser-estar-nuanced.pattern: ser = defining trait/norm · estar = perceived state/deviation from the norm
b2plus-ser-estar-nuanced.explanation: Beyond the classic "permanent vs temporary" rule, both verbs can describe the SAME adjective with a real meaning shift: "es guapo" (he's handsome — an inherent trait) versus "está guapo" (he looks handsome [right now, in that outfit] — a perceived state). "Es aburrido" (he's a boring person) versus "está aburrido" (he's bored right now). "Ser listo" (to be clever) versus "estar listo" (to be ready). The real distinction isn't duration — it's whether you're naming an inherent identity/norm (ser) or describing a perceived, comparable condition (estar).
b2plus-ser-estar-nuanced.fact: "Estar" is also the only option for location, no matter how permanent: "Madrid está en España" (Madrid is in Spain) uses "está" even though that fact never changes — location always takes "estar", one of the few genuinely fixed rules in this otherwise nuanced pair.

dialogue.native: ¡Qué guapa estás hoy! Ese vestido te queda increíble.
dialogue.en: You look so beautiful today! That dress looks amazing on you.

dialogue.native: Gracias, aunque tú siempre eres el más elegante del grupo.
dialogue.en: Thanks, though you're always the most elegant one in the group.

b2plus-compound-tenses.title: Compound Tenses Together: The Full Perfect System
b2plus-compound-tenses.pattern: he/había/habré/habría hablado — present/past/future/conditional perfect, all built the same way
b2plus-compound-tenses.explanation: Spanish has a full family of compound tenses, all built the same way (a form of "haber" + past participle), just with "haber" itself in a different tense: present perfect "he hablado" (I have spoken), past perfect "había hablado" (I had spoken), future perfect "habré hablado" (I will have spoken, by some future point), conditional perfect "habría hablado" (I would have spoken). Once you know the participle, all four tenses are just a matter of conjugating "haber" correctly.
b2plus-compound-tenses.fact: The future perfect also has the same probability use as the simple future: "Ya habrán llegado" doesn't just mean "they will have already arrived" — in casual speech it often means "they've probably already arrived," a guess about a completed action, not a genuine future prediction.

dialogue.native: Para cuando lleguemos, ya habrán empezado sin nosotros.
dialogue.en: By the time we arrive, they will have already started without us.

dialogue.native: Si hubiéramos salido antes, habríamos llegado a tiempo.
dialogue.en: If we had left earlier, we would have arrived on time.

b2plus-nominalization.title: Nominalization: Turning Verbs and Adjectives into Nouns
b2plus-nominalization.pattern: -ción/-miento/-dad/-eza (verb/adjective → noun), common in formal and written Spanish
b2plus-nominalization.explanation: Formal and written Spanish favors nouns where everyday speech uses verbs: instead of "decidimos rápido" (we decided quickly), a report might say "la rapidez de la decisión" (the speed of the decision). Common noun-forming suffixes: "-ción" (construir → construcción), "-miento" (crecer → crecimiento), "-dad" (posible → posibilidad), "-eza" (triste → tristeza). Recognizing these patterns unlocks a huge amount of formal vocabulary at once, since most of these nouns are entirely predictable from a verb or adjective you already know.
b2plus-nominalization.fact: This nominal style is sometimes criticized in style guides as "lenguaje burocrático" (bureaucratic language) when overused — native writers are taught that a strong verb ("decidieron rápido") often reads better than its noun version ("hubo rapidez en la decisión"), even though both are grammatically correct.

dialogue.native: La implementación del nuevo sistema requerirá varios meses.
dialogue.en: The implementation of the new system will require several months.

dialogue.native: Entiendo, aunque preferiría que simplemente nos dijeran cuándo van a implementarlo.
dialogue.en: I understand, although I'd prefer they just tell us when they're going to implement it.

c1-discourse-markers.title: Discourse Markers: Structuring a Sophisticated Argument
c1-discourse-markers.pattern: en primer lugar/por consiguiente/en definitiva/cabe destacar/en aras de
c1-discourse-markers.explanation: Native-level Spanish uses discourse markers to signal exactly how one idea relates to the next, the connective tissue of a well-built argument: "en primer lugar" (in the first place, to open a sequence), "por consiguiente" (consequently), "en definitiva" (ultimately, to summarize), "cabe destacar que" (it's worth highlighting that, to flag importance), "en aras de" (for the sake of, formal), "so pena de" (under penalty of, very formal/legal). These aren't just fancier synonyms for basic connectors — each signals a distinct logical function in an argument.
c1-discourse-markers.fact: "Cabe destacar" and its cousins "cabe señalar"/"cabe mencionar" (it's worth noting/mentioning) use the verb "caber" (to fit) in a fixed impersonal expression — literally "it fits to highlight," one of Spanish's many idiomatic uses of "caber" beyond its literal meaning of physical fit.

dialogue.native: Cabe destacar que, en aras de la transparencia, publicaremos todos los resultados.
dialogue.en: It's worth noting that, for the sake of transparency, we will publish all the results.

dialogue.native: En definitiva, es una decisión que beneficiará a todos por consiguiente.
dialogue.en: Ultimately, it's a decision that will consequently benefit everyone.

c1-idioms.title: Idiomatic Expressions: Sounding Like a Native
c1-idioms.pattern: fixed figurative phrases whose meaning can't be guessed from the individual words
c1-idioms.explanation: Idioms are where a language's personality really shows — phrases whose meaning has drifted completely from their literal words. "Costar un ojo de la cara" (to cost an eye from the face = to be very expensive), "estar en las nubes" (to be in the clouds = to be daydreaming), "tomar el pelo" (to take someone's hair = to tease/pull someone's leg), "meter la pata" (to put in the paw/leg = to mess up). These can't be decoded word-by-word — they simply have to be learned as fixed units.
c1-idioms.fact: Idioms are often surprisingly regional even within Latin American Spanish — "ni modo" (oh well, nothing to be done) is everyday Mexican Spanish, while "qué joda" (what a hassle) is distinctly Argentine/Uruguayan; a phrase can be instantly recognizable in one country and completely unfamiliar in another.

dialogue.native: Compré esta chaqueta y me costó un ojo de la cara.
dialogue.en: I bought this jacket and it cost me an arm and a leg.

dialogue.native: Bueno, no metas la pata la próxima vez y compara precios primero.
dialogue.en: Well, don't mess up next time and compare prices first.

c1-literary-register.title: Literary and Journalistic Register: Elevated Written Spanish
c1-literary-register.pattern: -se subjunctive forms · inverted word order · elevated vocabulary choices
c1-literary-register.explanation: Literary and journalistic Spanish reaches for the alternate -se subjunctive endings ("hablase" instead of "hablara") more often than everyday speech, and frequently inverts normal word order for emphasis or style: "Dijo el ministro que..." (Said the minister that... — verb before subject, common in news writing) instead of the conversational "El ministro dijo que...". Vocabulary also shifts upward: "acontecer" instead of "pasar" (to happen), "proceder a" instead of "empezar a" (to proceed to), "en tanto" instead of "mientras" (meanwhile).
c1-literary-register.fact: This register is what makes literature and newspapers feel noticeably more formal than spoken Spanish even when discussing the exact same events — much like how English news writing ("authorities stated") differs from casual speech ("they said") without changing the underlying grammar rules, just the register of the words chosen.

dialogue.native: Afirmó el portavoz que la decisión se tomaría en breve.
dialogue.en: The spokesperson stated that the decision would be made shortly.

dialogue.native: En tanto, la ciudadanía aguarda con expectación el desenlace.
dialogue.en: Meanwhile, the public awaits the outcome with anticipation.

c1-advanced-nominalization.title: Advanced Nominalization and the Gerund's Reach
c1-advanced-nominalization.pattern: el + infinitive (verb as noun) · gerund for cause/method/condition, without a conjunction
c1-advanced-nominalization.explanation: The infinitive itself can act as a noun when preceded by "el": "el saber no ocupa lugar" (knowing takes up no space — a proverb), "el vivir con incertidumbre" (living with uncertainty). Separately, the gerund (-ando/-iendo) can compress an entire subordinate clause into one word, replacing "porque", "si", or "con qué método" clauses: "Trabajando duro, logró su meta" (By working hard, he achieved his goal — method), "Sabiendo lo que sé ahora, no lo haría" (Knowing what I know now, I wouldn't do it — condition).
c1-advanced-nominalization.fact: This gerund-as-clause-compression is a hallmark of sophisticated written Spanish, but is easy to overuse — style guides warn against the "gerundio de posterioridad" (using a gerund for an action that happens AFTER the main verb, e.g. "salió corriendo, cayendo después"), which is considered incorrect; the gerund should describe something simultaneous or causal, not a subsequent event.

c2-proverbs.title: Proverbs (Refranes): Compressed Cultural Wisdom
c2-proverbs.pattern: fixed traditional sayings, often rhymed or rhythmic, carrying a moral or practical lesson
c2-proverbs.explanation: Refranes are centuries-old compressed wisdom, often built for memorability with rhyme or rhythm: "A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda" (God helps those who rise early), "En boca cerrada no entran moscas" (Flies don't enter a closed mouth = silence is often wise), "Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres" (Tell me who you walk with and I'll tell you who you are). Using one naturally, at the right moment, is one of the clearest markers of near-native fluency — they can't be improvised or translated, only known.
c2-proverbs.fact: Many refranes exist as rhyming pairs where the second half is often left unsaid because everyone already knows it — a native speaker might just say "a quien madruga..." and trail off, trusting the listener to mentally complete "Dios le ayuda", the same way English speakers might say "when in Rome..." without finishing the phrase.

dialogue.native: Llevo tres días levantándome a las cinco para terminar el proyecto.
dialogue.en: I've been getting up at five for three days to finish the project.

dialogue.native: Bueno, ya sabes lo que dicen: a quien madruga, Dios le ayuda.
dialogue.en: Well, you know what they say: God helps those who rise early.

c2-literary-allusion.title: Literary Allusion: Referencing a Shared Canon
c2-literary-allusion.pattern: brief references to well-known literary works/figures, used to compress meaning
c2-literary-allusion.explanation: At mastery level, speakers and writers reference well-known literary or cultural touchstones to compress a whole idea into a phrase, trusting the listener to fill in the rest: calling something "quijotesco" (quixotic, after Don Quijote) evokes noble but impractical idealism in a single word; "kafkiano" (Kafkaesque) evokes absurd, oppressive bureaucracy. These allusions function like idioms but draw specifically from literature rather than folk speech.
c2-literary-allusion.fact: "Como agua para chocolate" — literally "like water for chocolate," referring to water hot enough to make chocolate — is itself a common Spanish expression meaning someone is furious or emotionally boiling over, and it's also the title of a famous novel by Laura Esquivel, so the phrase carries a double resonance for readers.

dialogue.native: Todo este trámite burocrático es completamente kafkiano.
dialogue.en: This whole bureaucratic process is completely Kafkaesque.

dialogue.native: Sí, es una búsqueda tan quijotesca como inútil.
dialogue.en: Yes, it's as quixotic a quest as it is useless.

c2-register-shifting.title: Register-Shifting: Reading the Room in Real Time
c2-register-shifting.pattern: the same idea expressed at intimate/casual/professional/formal-ceremonial registers
c2-register-shifting.explanation: Mastery means fluidly moving between registers within a single conversation, the same way a native speaker toggles tone depending on who's listening. Telling a close friend something went badly might be "la cagué" (very crude/intimate); the same fact to a coworker might be "se me complicó un poco"; to a client, "hubo un contratiempo que ya estamos resolviendo"; at a formal ceremony, "lamentamos profundamente el inconveniente ocasionado." A C2 speaker chooses instinctively, without translating in their head.
c2-register-shifting.fact: Register mismatches are one of the most common ways an otherwise-fluent non-native speaker gets flagged as foreign — using a stiff, textbook-formal phrase with close friends (or, worse, a crude/intimate phrase in a professional setting) reads as more of a tell than any grammar mistake, because native speakers rarely consciously notice register — they just feel when it's wrong.

dialogue.native: Tranquilo, se lo explicamos al cliente como que hubo un pequeño contratiempo.

readingPassage.context: A literary, mastery-level narrative.

paragraphs.native: El viejo cartógrafo, habiendo dedicado su vida entera a dibujar fronteras ajenas, decidió, en sus últimos años, trazar un mapa de su propia memoria.
paragraphs.en: The old cartographer, having dedicated his entire life to drawing others' borders, decided, in his final years, to map his own memory.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que aquel mapa no señalaba montañas ni ríos, sino los lugares exactos donde había sido feliz.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting that map didn't mark mountains or rivers, but the exact places where he had been happy.

paragraphs.native: De no haberse atrevido a esta última obra, tan íntima y distinta de todas las anteriores, habría muerto sin conocerse verdaderamente a sí mismo.
paragraphs.en: Had he not dared this final work, so intimate and different from all his previous ones, he would have died without truly knowing himself.

paragraphs.native: Sus hijos, encontrando aquel mapa después de su muerte, comprendieron que el verdadero territorio de un hombre no son las tierras que recorre, sino los instantes que atesora.
paragraphs.en: His children, finding that map after his death, understood that a man's true territory is not the lands he travels, but the moments he treasures.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, aquel último mapa, sin coordenadas ni escalas, resultó ser la obra más precisa que jamás había dibujado.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, that final map, without coordinates or scale, turned out to be the most precise work he had ever drawn.

paragraphs.native: En aquel pueblo, que tenía un aire casi a Macondo, todos sabían que la anciana hablaba con los árboles, aunque nadie se atrevía a preguntarle qué le respondían.
paragraphs.en: In that town, which had an almost Macondo-like air, everyone knew the old woman talked to the trees, although no one dared ask her what they answered.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que, desde que ella cuidaba del bosque, ningún árbol había vuelto a enfermar ni a morir sin razón aparente.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting that, since she started tending the forest, no tree had gotten sick or died without apparent reason again.

paragraphs.native: De haberla llamado loca, como hicieron algunos forasteros, se habrían perdido la sabiduría silenciosa que aquella mujer guardaba.
paragraphs.en: Had they called her crazy, as some outsiders did, they would have missed the silent wisdom that woman held.

paragraphs.native: Sabiendo que pronto moriría, enseñó a su nieta todo lo que los árboles le habían susurrado durante décadas.
paragraphs.en: Knowing she would soon die, she taught her granddaughter everything the trees had whispered to her for decades.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, cuando la anciana murió, el pueblo entero juró haber escuchado, esa misma noche, un susurro colectivo entre las hojas.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, when the old woman died, the whole town swore they heard, that very night, a collective whisper among the leaves.

lessons.description: A story of register-shifting and diplomatic restraint.

paragraphs.native: Durante la negociación más tensa de su carrera, el diplomático, en lugar de responder con la misma agresividad que recibía, simplemente guardó silencio.
paragraphs.en: During the most tense negotiation of his career, the diplomat, instead of responding with the same aggression he received, simply remained silent.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que aquel silencio, prolongado durante casi un minuto entero, desarmó por completo a su interlocutor.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting that silence, prolonged for almost an entire minute, completely disarmed his counterpart.

paragraphs.native: De haber respondido con la misma dureza, aquella reunión, so pena de romperse irreparablemente, jamás habría llegado a un acuerdo.

paragraphs.native: Sabiendo exactamente cuándo hablar y cuándo callar, logró, en definitiva, lo que ningún argumento elocuente habría conseguido.
paragraphs.en: Knowing exactly when to speak and when to be silent, he achieved, ultimately, what no eloquent argument could have accomplished.

paragraphs.native: Aquel día, sus colegas comprendieron que la verdadera maestría diplomática reside, a menudo, en el arte del silencio bien calculado.

lessons.title: A Proverb for Every Season
lessons.description: A reflective story built around proverbs woven into narration.

readingPassage.context: A reflective story built around proverbs woven into narration.

paragraphs.native: Mi abuelo tenía un refrán para cada ocasión, y con los años comprendí que, en el fondo, eran su forma particular de filosofía.
paragraphs.en: My grandfather had a proverb for every occasion, and over the years I understood that, deep down, they were his particular form of philosophy.

paragraphs.native: Cuando algo salía mal, decía: no hay mal que por bien no venga, y, sorprendentemente, casi siempre tenía razón.
paragraphs.en: When something went wrong, he would say: every cloud has a silver lining, and, surprisingly, he was almost always right.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que jamás usaba esos refranes para minimizar el dolor ajeno, sino para ofrecer, con delicadeza, una perspectiva más amplia.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting he never used those proverbs to minimize others' pain, but to gently offer a broader perspective.

paragraphs.native: De no haber heredado esa costumbre suya, quizás jamás habría aprendido a encontrar sabiduría en el lenguaje más sencillo.
paragraphs.en: Had I not inherited that habit of his, I might never have learned to find wisdom in the simplest language.

paragraphs.native: Hoy, cuando repito sus refranes a mis propios hijos, siento que mi abuelo, en cierto modo, sigue hablando a través de mí.
paragraphs.en: Today, when I repeat his proverbs to my own children, I feel that my grandfather, in a way, still speaks through me.

paragraphs.native: En su lecho de muerte, el compositor, habiendo escrito sinfonías enteras a lo largo de su vida, pidió que no se tocara ninguna música.
paragraphs.en: On his deathbed, the composer, having written entire symphonies throughout his life, asked that no music be played.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que quería, por primera vez en décadas, escuchar el silencio absoluto sin ninguna melodía compitiendo por su atención.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting he wanted, for the first time in decades, to hear absolute silence without any melody competing for his attention.

paragraphs.native: De no haber dedicado toda una vida al sonido, quizás jamás habría comprendido la belleza casi musical del silencio mismo.
paragraphs.en: Had he not dedicated a whole life to sound, he might never have understood the almost musical beauty of silence itself.

paragraphs.native: Sus alumnos, respetando su última voluntad, permanecieron junto a él sin pronunciar una sola palabra hasta el final.
paragraphs.en: His students, respecting his last wish, stayed by his side without saying a single word until the end.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, aquel hombre que había dedicado su existencia a llenar el mundo de música, eligió despedirse en el silencio más puro.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, that man who had dedicated his existence to filling the world with music chose to say goodbye in the purest silence.

lessons.title: The Village Where No One Lied

readingPassage.context: A philosophical, almost fable-like story.

paragraphs.native: Cuenta la leyenda que existió un pueblo donde, por alguna razón jamás explicada, nadie era capaz de mentir.
paragraphs.en: Legend has it there once existed a town where, for some never-explained reason, no one was capable of lying.

paragraphs.native: Cabe preguntarse si aquella honestidad absoluta era, en realidad, una bendición o una maldición disfrazada.
paragraphs.en: One might ask whether that absolute honesty was, in reality, a blessing or a disguised curse.

paragraphs.native: De no haber podido mentir jamás, ni siquiera por cortesía, las relaciones de aquel pueblo se volvieron sorprendentemente frágiles.
paragraphs.en: Had they never been able to lie, not even out of courtesy, that town's relationships became surprisingly fragile.

paragraphs.native: Con el tiempo, sus habitantes aprendieron que la verdad, sin la más mínima compasión, puede resultar tan destructiva como cualquier mentira.
paragraphs.en: Over time, its inhabitants learned that truth, without the slightest compassion, can be as destructive as any lie.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, aquella fábula nos enseña que la honestidad verdadera requiere, además de valentía, una buena dosis de ternura.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, that fable teaches us that true honesty requires, besides courage, a good dose of tenderness.

options: They became perfect

exercises.question: What lesson does the fable teach?
options: Lying is always good
True honesty requires courage and tenderness

Nothing meaningful

lessons.title: The Letter Written in Two Languages
lessons.titleNative: La carta escrita en dos idiomas
lessons.description: A story about bilingual identity and the untranslatable.

readingPassage.context: A story about bilingual identity and the untranslatable.

paragraphs.native: Escribió la primera mitad de la carta en su lengua materna y la segunda en español, sabiendo que solo así podría expresar completamente lo que sentía.
paragraphs.en: She wrote the first half of the letter in her mother tongue and the second in Spanish, knowing only that way could she fully express what she felt.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que ciertas emociones, para ella, simplemente no existían del todo en un solo idioma.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting that certain emotions, for her, simply didn't fully exist in a single language.

paragraphs.native: De haber escrito la carta enteramente en un solo idioma, algo esencial se habría perdido irremediablemente en el proceso.
paragraphs.en: Had she written the letter entirely in a single language, something essential would have been irretrievably lost in the process.

paragraphs.native: Quien la leyó, aun sin dominar ambos idiomas por igual, sintió, de alguna manera, la totalidad de lo que ella había querido decir.
paragraphs.en: Whoever read it, even without mastering both languages equally, somehow felt the entirety of what she had wanted to say.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, aquella carta demostró que el amor, a veces, necesita más de un idioma para expresarse por completo.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, that letter proved that love sometimes needs more than one language to fully express itself.

options: That translation is easy
That love sometimes needs more than one language
That one language is always enough
Nothing important

lessons.title: The Chess Player's Final Move
lessons.description: A story about wisdom, patience, and mastery.

readingPassage.context: A story about wisdom, patience, and mastery.

paragraphs.native: El viejo maestro de ajedrez, habiendo jugado miles de partidas a lo largo de su vida, tardó casi una hora en decidir su último movimiento.
paragraphs.en: The old chess master, having played thousands of games throughout his life, took nearly an hour to decide his final move.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que sus rivales más jóvenes, impacientes por naturaleza, jamás comprendieron el valor de tanta paciencia.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting his younger rivals, impatient by nature, never understood the value of so much patience.

paragraphs.native: De haber movido apresuradamente, como tantas veces le sugirieron, habría sacrificado una victoria construida durante toda una vida de reflexión.
paragraphs.en: Had he moved hastily, as he was so often urged to, he would have sacrificed a victory built over a lifetime of reflection.

paragraphs.native: Sabiendo que aquella sería probablemente su última gran partida, quiso saborear cada segundo antes de anunciar el jaque mate.
paragraphs.en: Knowing that would probably be his last great game, he wanted to savor every second before announcing checkmate.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, aquel movimiento final resumió, en un solo instante, toda una filosofía de vida basada en la paciencia.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, that final move summed up, in a single instant, an entire life philosophy based on patience.

exercises.question: What did his final move summarize?

lessons.title: The Bridge Between Two Worlds
lessons.description: A reflective story on immigration, identity, and belonging.

readingPassage.context: A reflective story on immigration, identity, and belonging.

paragraphs.native: Habiendo cruzado la frontera con apenas una maleta y un idioma que no dominaba del todo, jamás imaginó que algún día se sentiría en casa en ambos lados.
paragraphs.en: Having crossed the border with barely a suitcase and a language he didn't fully master, he never imagined he would someday feel at home on both sides.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que, con los años, dejó de sentirse dividido entre dos identidades y empezó a sentirse, más bien, enriquecido por ambas.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting that, over the years, he stopped feeling divided between two identities and began to feel, rather, enriched by both.

paragraphs.native: De no haber perseverado durante aquellos primeros años tan difíciles, jamás habría llegado a convertirse en ese puente viviente entre dos culturas.
paragraphs.en: Had he not persevered through those very difficult early years, he would never have become that living bridge between two cultures.

paragraphs.native: Sus propios hijos, criados ya en ambos idiomas desde la cuna, heredaron sin esfuerzo la riqueza que a él le costó tanto construir.
paragraphs.en: His own children, raised in both languages from the cradle, effortlessly inherited the richness it took him so much to build.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres, pero él, con orgullo, terminó andando con ambos mundos a la vez.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, tell me who you walk with and I'll tell you who you are, but he, proudly, ended up walking with both worlds at once.

lessons.title: The Final Lesson
lessons.description: A capstone reflective story reviewing the full arc of C2 mastery.

readingPassage.context: A capstone reflective story reviewing the full arc of C2 mastery.

paragraphs.native: Habiendo enseñado español durante toda una vida, la maestra se preparaba para dar su última clase antes de jubilarse.
paragraphs.en: Having taught Spanish her whole life, the teacher was preparing to give her last class before retiring.

paragraphs.native: Cabe destacar que, en lugar de repasar gramática, decidió simplemente contarles a sus alumnos lo que el idioma le había enseñado a ella.
paragraphs.en: It's worth noting that, instead of reviewing grammar, she decided to simply tell her students what the language had taught her.

paragraphs.native: De no haber dedicado su vida a este idioma, jamás habría comprendido que aprender una lengua es, en el fondo, aprender a amar de una manera nueva.
paragraphs.en: Had she not dedicated her life to this language, she would never have understood that learning a language is, deep down, learning to love in a new way.

paragraphs.native: Sabiendo que probablemente no volvería a verlos, les dijo, con la voz quebrada: el saber no ocupa lugar, pero el amor por aprender ocupa toda una vida.
paragraphs.en: Knowing she probably wouldn't see them again, she told them, her voice breaking: knowledge takes up no space, but the love of learning fills an entire lifetime.

paragraphs.native: En definitiva, aquel día, sus alumnos comprendieron que habían aprendido mucho más que gramática y vocabulario: habían aprendido a habitar un idioma entero.
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, that day, her students understood they had learned much more than grammar and vocabulary: they had learned to inhabit an entire language.
